utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Barriot. I must remind you that you took an oath at the beginning or made a declaration at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, but nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we were still talking yesterday, you and I, when we knocked off and I was trying to understand from you that you are a man of honour, you sacrificed your profession as a soldier for the sake of the truth, and then you wrote this article which, according to your testimony, misrepresents the role played by Mr. Martic in the shelling of Zagreb. You are aware of this -- what are you going to do about it? What have you done to correct this misinformation to the public?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that there has been some confusion in what we said. I do not believe it is a problem of interpretation because the interpretation is excellent, so maybe I misspoke. So allow me to go back on my explanations. In May 1995, when the Orkan rockets were launched on Zagreb the official version was that Mr. Milan Martic had ordered the firing. That was the official version, the one I received initially. But very soon thereafter, as I told you, I heard that the Orkan rockets were targeting objects, structures, as I said yesterday. I also said that if President Milan Martic had made that decision it was because he did not want a subordinate to be held responsible for the firing. As a president he wanted to take that responsibility and that decision. This is something I learned later. At any rate, I never changed what I had written. I maintain what I have written because that was the official version. That was the one President Martic had agreed to. Later on, I realised that he wasn't the one who had made the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, sir? I understand all what you are telling me. What I'm asking you is what have you done since you became aware of the correct version to correct the impression that you gave to the world?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm doing it today here before this Tribunal, because you put the question to me, and I respond. I reply faithful to my conscious and to my belief and to what I know. Now, if Mr. Milan Martic is asking me -- or were to ask me to change statement, I would do so, but I convey to you what was really -- what my soul and conscience was telling me. I lost everything to tell the truth. I broke my career, broke my relationship. I have no interest in saying anything that would be the opposite of the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is -- yes, but I hear that you're saying you are correcting your mistake here in court, but your mistake here in court is only going to be heard by those who read the case -- the record of the case. Those who read your article will not come to know of your correction, and usually when we do make corrections of things that we put in the media, the idea is to make that correction in the same medium that we used when we first made the mistake.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm willing to do so, but I do not believe it is that relevant. I believe what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are very right, it is not that relevant. My question actually is not in the future. I'm not asking you what you are going to do. I was asking what you had done to correct because of your conscience, as a man of truth. Now, obviously to date you have done nothing except what you have said in court. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I believe this is the most important thing, to tell the truth on my honour in court and in front of you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I just ask, what the contents of what you said today really mean when you said you later learned that the official version was not the right one. So first, what do you mean? You said the official version was Milan Martic, the accused in this case, ordered that shelling. That can mean two things; that she ordered -- that he ordered to hit the targets which were hit at the end of the day or to indiscriminately shell Zagreb; or it can mean that somebody else gave the order, because what you said was ambiguous, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I was not clear in my statement because it is clear in my mind. I learned later on in the entourage of Mr. Martic and through discussion that he wasn't the one who had ordered the shelling but he had taken responsibility for it because the decision had been made by a subordinate, and as a president he did not want a subordinate to be held responsible for a decision that he as a president had not taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So who was it who had taken the decision, according to what you had learned later?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, sir. I'm not familiar enough with the chain of command in the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I asked you what you learned later. You said you learned that it was not the accused Milan Martic who gave the order. So was that also part of what you learned, who else gave the order? I don't mean you have to know enough about the chain of command, but just --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I do not know the name, but I know he was a subordinate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And the function and the direct subordinate or whatever, you know nothing again? Again, I'm asking you once more.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm very sorry, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just on this last point that Mr. Milan Martic took the responsibility as the president. You'd agree that in fact responsibility would go to him as the president in fact and in law. Isn't it so? By virtue of being the president.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In law, and also in honour, because it was a matter of defending a civilian population against an aggression, and it was self-defence. It was only logical and honourable to take on that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a very brief one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Barriot, yesterday in responding to the Trial Chamber's questions, and I believe also during the cross-examination you referred to Muslim refugees from, as you put it, the so-called Bihac pocket. You refer to it a number of 40.000 such refugees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Bench, Mr. Perovic. I don't seem to remember any of the Judges asking about the Muslims, but you can remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Moloto, it seems to me that you asked about Muslim refugees in the RSK and their position in the RSK. And as far as I can remember, you asked why hadn't they gone to Croatia, and my question is actually in connection with that part of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, so if I understood you well, these are Muslim refugees from a neighbouring country, Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They came from the Bihac pocket, from the area of Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, these are not people who lived in the RSK before that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They can be regarded as refugees in RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And if I got it right, as refugees they found refuge in the RSK, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. They came to seek refuge in the Betanija and Turan camps, and I can tell you I was there on those occasions. I visited those camps. I saw the refugees with -- especially with Mr. Bertrand Dupasquier, who was responsible for the UNHCR. We did see all these refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Moloto asked you why had not those people gone to Croatia from Bosnia. In that connection, I will ask you this question: Do you know what the position was of the Croatian authorities towards a possible transfer of those refugees from the Bihac pocket to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Perovic, the question was why don't they go to other parts of former Yugoslavia where -- whether the economic situation was better than in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand this, Mr. Barriot, the clarification of this question by His Honour? So yesterday the question actually was why had they gone to the RSK. Why had not they gone to Serbia, Croatia or any other part of the former Yugoslavia? Can you tell us why didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a very simple reason. It was the closest region where they could be accepted, and also it was not okay for the Croatian authorities to welcome Muslim refugees. .

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said where they could be accepted, right? Thank you. Thank you. You have answered my question in advance, as a matter of fact. I have no further questions for you, Mr. Barriot. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I switched seats today. I will. I just have a couple of quick questions, Mr. Barriot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll try. It's kind of uncomfortable with a short microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, isn't true that Muslims fleeing from Serb areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina went to Croatia? So not talking about the Bihac pocket but other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were Muslims who fled to Croatia; correct? Or do you not know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I know the situation perfectly well. You seem to forget one thing. At the time, Mr. Fikret Abdic, since September 1993, had proclaimed the autonomous province of Western Bosnia, so these were people faithful, Muslims faithful to Fikret Abdic. So the government of Izetbegovic and the 5th Corps wanted to eliminate them. So from where they were in the Bihac pocket they could not go anywhere else in Bosnia because they would have been killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. My question was about places other than the Bihac pocket, and actually I haven't forgotten anything you said. But can you answer my question about whether Muslims fleeing other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina in fact went to Croatia. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no, or else they were in very few numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you about something else which His Honour Judge Moloto asked you about today and it was about whether you made any corrections to the statement about Mr. Martic ordering the shelling of Zagreb. In fact, not only did you not correct that, but you repeated it by publishing the article in September of 1997 and again in this book in 2003 Our Testimonies about Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there was no reason for changing what had been written, none at all. These writings, I'm not testifying before a Tribunal, in court, but I'm doing that today here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Isn't the real explanation is there was no reason for changing it because it was true and correct, and the only reason you're now changing your story today is that you're just afraid that you'll do some damage to Mr. Martic's defence case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's absolutely wrong. You are putting words in my mouth that don't belong to me. I described the responsibility taken on by President Martic. Today I'm being asked of what I know and what my conscience tells me. These are two different things. I never had some kind of dual standards in my speeches and statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Barriot, this brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for taking the time off to come and testify in this Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Defence would like to call the next witness, Nikola Dobrijevic. Nikola Dobrijevic will also testify viva voce, just like Mr. Barriot. The reasons for proceeding this way are the same as in the case of Mr. Barriot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I hope this won't count as a housekeeping matter because that would mean I've broken my pledge, but I don't think it is. I have a -- just two small matters to raise with respect to this witness. The first is very easily resolved, I think, and the second one may be more difficult. We received a detailed 65 ter summary for this witness approximately an hour and 15 minutes before court started today. Previously we had received a very extremely short and extremely vague 65 ter summary, and it was only, as I said, an hour and 15 minutes before court started that we received this two-page detailed 65 ter summary. I have copies of it if Your Honours -- I know that it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would appreciate it because mine is in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. With the assistance of the usher, I have a number of copies. And there are kind of two matters related to this. The first is quite obviously the timing, and then the second matter is the substance of some of the matters that are in the -- in the 65 ter summary. With respect to timing, obviously receiving it an hour ago, or an hour and 15 minutes ago is not really enough time for us. If I'm permitted to start my cross-examination on Monday, it's fine, I can prepare and that will be no problem. So that issue is eliminated as long as I don't have to start crossing until Monday. And I don't believe, actually, that's going to be a problem because I think the next witness is not scheduled to start until Tuesday at the earliest. So that's the one -- that's easy to resolve, if Your Honours agree, and if Defence counsel does not object. The other one that may be more difficult is, I do note on the 65 ter summary there are a number of topics which -- which we would submit are covered by Your Honours' ruling of I believe last week of matters that Your Honours do not want to hear more evidence about, and there are other matters which are frankly, in our view, irrelevant, go to tu quoque or are just really outside the scope -- or not relevant to the charges in the indictment. I don't know if Your Honours would like to go through briefly the summary and indicate beforehand which matters maybe should not be explored to make things easier so we don't have to sort of jump up and fight about it or -- that's just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say there are issues that are irrelevant, you mean in this latest statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which I didn't have time to look at it before we came into court anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. And I think it's the -- I think the latest statement is really the one that governs. I think it's -- yeah. I don't even know if there are matters on the earlier one that are going to be addressed that are not contained in the latest statement. I think all the matters are in the latest 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any response to the two issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very briefly, Your Honour. Everything that my learned colleague said on the time when they received this summary is correct, and the Defence is in agreement if the Chamber wishes so that Prosecution cross-examines the witness on Monday. This was done, this late submission of the 65 ter summary, because of the rescheduling of some other witnesses, and this is what will explain, and we apologise for that to our learned colleague from the Prosecution. With reference to the tu quoque defence, the defence is -- this should not be used, this prohibition, to preclude Defence from defending the accused. Everything in this statement which refers to the witness's statement, everything refers to the status of affairs on Banija, the area of the RSK about which we haven't heard anything so far, no testimony, apart from what happened in one, two, or three villages, and what happened on a certain date. This witness is going to explain what happened in the area which is covered by the indictment in a chronological order. He doesn't deal principally -- in a principal manner with the elections, formation of the Zengas, the Z-4 plan, none of the matters that we were instructed about, not to dwell again on that. And the very end of this summary, pointed out by the Prosecution, concerns issues that have not been covered so far, and this is going to be an original statement of the witness on what he knows, and I believe that these are very important issues for the Bench and for the -- for these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Any response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before Mr. Black responds -- sorry, Mr. Whiting, my apologies. Mr. Milovancevic, I have not understood your response clearly in respect to the issue of tu quoque. Could I get it with somewhat more clarity? I'm not able to see whether you're accepting what Mr. Whiting says. You're saying you would be able to lead such a defence and raise such a defence and establish it, seek to establish it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I'm very sorry if I lacked precision. What I wanted to say is that we believe that objection to tu quoque defence is not a valid one. We are not doing that, this is our opinion, and that use of such an objection could be used or misused to preclude the proper functioning of the defence. Have I been more precise or more clear this time round?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But to preclude the proper functioning of the defence in relation to which specific issues and which specific evidence from the defence? Because you seem to be saying it should not be used as that specific defence but that the evidence that would form the foundation for it could be used in a different context in relation to the whole of the defence case, and that's what I want to be clear on, because there is some ambivalence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for this question. Well, Defence's stance is that it has not tried to use tu quoque on any occasion so far. And when I said this a couple of minutes ago, I wanted to say is that what we are trying to paint a realistic picture in the area and in the relevant time period of the indictment and not to view facts outside their context, isolated from their context. We want to consider things within the context so that we can -- may draw conclusions what both sides wanted. And this is why I said what I said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. I appreciate it. It's much clearer to me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black -- Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm flattered by the confusion. But I'm flattered because it's young and old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would just note that there are a number of paragraphs which could, and I really leave it up to Your Honours, fall under the ruling of the Chamber last week. For example, just after the four sort of short introductory paragraphs, there is a sentence about the referendum in the summer of 1990. Then the next paragraph is about the MUP of Croatia allegedly raiding Petrinja in September of 1990. Then -- then there's another paragraph and then there's a paragraph about the 26th of June, 1991, Croatia proclaims independence and Croatian forces in Kostajnica. Then the next paragraph is about Croatian troops. Then the next paragraph is about alleged crimes against Serbs in Sisak. Then there are a number -- on the second page there are a number of paragraphs which do go to issues in the indictment. But then the last three paragraphs, the --the first of the last three paragraphs is about -- is about Stipe Mesic and Croatia proclaiming independence, and then the last two paragraphs are about Operation Storm and events occurring after Operation Storm and just shortly before Operation Storm. Now, it seems to me that some if not all of those paragraphs that I have identified fall under the Court's ruling, but again I just -- I leave it up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. I think we must get on to the witness now, and I must make a ruling. On the first point that you raised, before I rule on that one, can we get an assurance that if the Prosecution is going to start cross on Monday that we will finish with that witness on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Completely finish. Judges' questions, questions arising from Judges' questions, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Assuming that the witness finishes his direct examination today, I would think, judging on what I've seen, that I could do the cross-examination in two sessions, leaving a third -- a full entire third session for re-examination and Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then that being the case, then the Prosecution will be given the opportunity to start its cross-examination on Monday. On the second issue, precisely because the Chamber has not had sufficient time to read this, and I know it's not a very long statement but it's not been possible to read it in between I had time to listen to the arguments, I would think -- would like to leave it to counsel to jump up when irrelevant issues are being raised or issues that have been mentioned in the order of a couple of days ago are mentioned. Just jump up in the normal course. Okay? Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic. You may call the witness, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: None of the booths have the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: None of them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: None of the interpreters' booths have the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't know that the interpreters get the summary usually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It's not necessary for the interpreters. It will not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Dobrijevic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You know my name. My name is Predrag Milovancevic, Defence counsel for Mr. Milan Martic, and on behalf of the Defence team I'm going to examine you today. Before I start asking questions, I'm going to ask you to be mindful, and I will be mindful as well, to leave a gap between questions and answers so that the interpreters may have the time to interpret what we are saying. We have to assist them in that. Thank you very much in advance. And I'm trying to put to you shorter questions and you try to give me short answers.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us your full name and where you were born.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm Nikola Dobrijevic. I was born on the 7th of September, 1950, in the village of Bestrma. I'm a jurist. I fathered two grown-up children and currently I'm living in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you're a jurist. Am I right when I conclude that you graduated from law school?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did graduate from law school. I was the best in class.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us your -- something about your career, positions you held before 1990.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I worked in the steelworks in Sisak as a metalworker. Later on I graduated from machine-work school, and as a scholar of Tito's fund I graduated from law school. Later on I was a trainee judge at the court in Sisak, and then as a manager in Autopromet Sisak, and then later on I came back to the steelworks of Sisak in the legal department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I ask which law school you graduated from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The school in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sorry for interrupting. Please, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As we are now talking about your curriculum vitae, perhaps it would be good for you to tell us what offices you held or what duties you discharged from 1990 to 1995 in the area of the SAO Krajina and then the republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, I joined the Territorial Defence, and I was on the Territorial Defence Staff in Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will suffice. When I put to you this question a while ago, I was referring to political offices. Did you hold any political posts? Were you a deputy, a director, a minister anywhere?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the war I was one of the organisers of the Socialist Party of Croatia, a pro-Yugoslav party, a party of Yugoslav orientation, which was established in Petrinja between two election cycles in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever a deputy? I should like to ask you that directly.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a deputy to the Assembly of the republic of the Serbian Krajina from the beginning up to the 1990 elections -- 1993 elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Krajina Suma, does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: After my function ceased in the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina, I was an assistant director of the enterprise Krajina Suma until the Storm operation, and also I was a minister in the cabinet of the late Prime Minister Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a while ago after my function in the MUP ceased I became assistant director of the director of Krajina Suma. So what did you do in the MUP of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: For a short while, towards the end of 1992 and in early 1993, I was the MUP coordinator for Banija in the Ministry of the Interior of the Krajina. So that in a certain way I was an assistant to Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall try to follow a chronology of events which could be of interest. You mentioned the Socialist Party of Croatia, a party of a Yugoslav orientation. Can you tell us when was this party established and by whom?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: That party was established in 1990 between two election cycles in Croatia. In view of the fact that Ivica Racan practically was the greatest delusion for the Krajina Serbs, in particular the Banija Serbs, he won the elections in the first round primarily thanks to the votes of the Banija Serbs, and in the second round he completely changed the platform of his party and, among other things, emphasised that Croatian sovereignty was indivisible, which meant that the Serbs would be struck out from the constitution of Croatia and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Am I wrong to conclude that at the time of the first multi-party elections in Croatia you were one of the founders of the Socialist Party of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I should stress that there were a large number of Croats there as well, and the secretary of the party was Goran Babic, a Croatian writer from the island Vis. And there were another -- a number of renowned persons, figures from the socio-political life of Croatia, including from Croatian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know anything about the conducting of a referendum on the sovereignty of the Serbian people in the Krajina and in Croatia? Do you remember anything about it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember that referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I'm just interested in one thing in connection with the referendum, who had the right to participate in the referendum. It was a referendum on the autonomy and sovereignty of the Serbian people in Croatia. Who had the right to take part in it? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Where I come from where the population is more or less mixed, it is Serb or Croat, or Croat or Serb, as you like it. All the people who lived there had the right to take part in the referendum. So to be quite clear, I'm speaking of the area of Banija mostly, the centre of which is Sisak, and the municipalities are Petrinja, Glina, Kostajnica, Dvor Na Uni, and Novska was also a part of it for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for this short pause, Your Honours. For your easy reference, it is on page 21 in squares C3 and D3 in the atlas that we are using that you can see the towns that will be referred to by this witness. So it is page 21 in the atlas that we are using. Mr. Dobrijevic, I shall now ask you this question: What larger towns are there in Banija? What are the key towns in the area?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just enumerated them. Sisak, Petrinja, Kostajnica, Glina, Dvor Na Uni.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many inhabitants this area had in 1990 and what its ethnic mix was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Around 200.000 inhabitants, of which about 48 per cent were Croats, 36 per cent Serbs, 12 Yugoslavs, and the rest were others. However, as established in a later census, the Yugoslavs were mainly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: But if the Bench shall allow me, I am talking also about the city of Sisak, which stretches all the way up to Velika Gorica, to Zagreb, and this is exclusively Croatian population. But in Banija where the republic of the Serbian Krajina was was a majority Serbian area, but Sisak belonged to Croatia and not to Krajina. I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying the city of Sisak stretches all the way to Velika Gorica, or are you talking about the municipal area moving up in that direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sisak stretches all the way up to Velika Gorica. It borders on Velika Gorica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When we speak about all these places in Banija, do you know what party won at the first multi-party elections in 1990 in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object on the ground that I indicated earlier, that this is, it seems to me, on the list of topics that the Chamber doesn't need to hear more information on. It specifically included multi-party elections -- sorry, the multi-party election.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point I'm not dealing with the multi-party elections in the political sense or as a matter of principle. I'm just talking about the election results in a specific town. And the result and the figures that will be obtained for the municipality of Kostajnica will be very interesting. This is something which the Chamber should know. And that is the sole question that I shall be putting in connection with the elections. Just because of this figure, this fact which has not been referred to so far in the proceedings, and we do have a count in the indictment which relates to Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, if -- if -- if this specific question Defence counsel thinks is so important, then I guess fine, let it go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You heard my question, Mr. Dobrijevic. So who won in Kostajnica at the first multi-party elections, and who was the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: That is a very interesting question, because in Kostajnica Racan's SDP won, and out of the 56 seats only six were Croats. All the others were Serbs. And a Croat, Slavko Miocevic was elected president of the municipality in Kostajnica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were the international -- nationality, inter-ethnic and inter-personal relations like in Banija, in Kostajnica in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: There was already some tension in their relations in 1990 because the first arming had already started by the Croatian paramilitaries. But as regards ordinary people, their inter-personal relations were like before. There was nothing -- there were no particular tensions among the ordinary folk, but one could observe because of the very emergence of the HDZ on the political scene of Croatia there could be observed some tensions also in the area of Banija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When -- as one of the larger places in Banija in autumn, at the end of September 1990, Petrinja is mentioned. Can you tell us what associations you have in that respect?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Petrinja was very interesting because of the Gavrilovic meat packing industry, one of the largest meat industries in Croatia, and it was the spearhead of economic development generally speaking in the area. Apart from that, the Croatian party, Socialist Party, the Yugoslav-oriented party, had its seat in Petrinja. At the end of 1990, I believe it was in September, I cannot recall the exact date, this point was launched, the well-known operation by the Croatian police, the Croatian redarstvenici, namely to pick up all the reserve force police weapons from the police stations in places where the majority population were Serbs. This was, I believe, in September 1990, and this is when the first serious tensions in Banija emerged with 400 people fleeing to barracks after which 300 armed ZNG members whom we called the MUP members at the time arrived in Petrinja, and the arrests started. A hundred people were arrested on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we are talking about late September 1990. You have given me a lengthy answer about those events. In your assessment, why did the Croatian MUP intervene in Petrinja? What was the direct cause to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the direct cause was the disarming of these police stations in Banija in places where there was a Serb majority population, and in view of the fact that the people had learned that the weaponry, the armaments, were to be taken to Sisak by night. And before that, Ljubo Loncarovic, who was a Serb and was the chief of police in Petrinja, he had been taken already in the morning of that day to Sisak in order not to be present when this was taking place, and they attempted to take the weapons to Sisak by night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, tell us to whom did those armaments in the police station in Petrinja belong?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: To the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How was that -- the arms to be transferred to Sisak?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a van with Zagreb licence plates, which was intercepted at the exit from Petrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have already answered my question, but I will ask you. Who intercepted that vehicle and why?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It was intercepted by activists of the Serbian Democratic Party because they were the only ones who had that information - I don't know from where - that the weapons in question would be dislocated, i.e., transferred to Sisak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what happened with the weapons after that. Was it taken to Sisak or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. The armaments were returned, and after that, as I said, 300 policemen came from Zagreb, and using, so to speak, their Ustasha methods they tried -- they started searching houses, stabbing through pillows, arrested people before the eyes of children. They arrested some 300 people, and the individuals even spent time in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That will do. Mr. Dobrijevic, you said a while ago that special members -- unit members came and arrested people according to Ustasha methods. Why did you use that kind of a term?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that they were such methods, but they were completely uncivilised at any rate. They had bayonets on their rifles. They barged into houses. They pierced pillows. They looked through haystacks. They went to the attics of houses and so on and so forth. And they arrested the parents and took them away in front of their minor children. So I don't know how else to actually describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Were there any reactions to the arrest of so many people and such an action on the part of the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We immediately, as the Socialist Party, the socialist Croat party, a party of Yugoslav orientation, we immediately informed the federal leadership, the Presidency, the army, and I believe that Petar Gracanin was the chief of the federal police at that time. He was being treated at the VMA hospital, and we informed him about what had happened in Petrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was it that you wanted to achieve by sending that information? You as a party informed the state leadership about the problem. What were you looking for?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We were looking for assistance, for help from the federal organs. We understood that this policy in Croatia was so wayward that we could not expect help from anyone there, and we expected the federal organs to take steps to prevent this illegal behaviour from what were already some paramilitary units of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any reaction from the federal authorities?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that three days later Vasil Tupurkovski, a Presidency member, came. But he had met Stipo Mesic at the Pleso airport before coming to us and collected information from Mesic and then arrived to Petrinja. I wasn't at that meeting because in the meantime we had organised a rally in the village of Banski Grabovac. There were tens of thousands of people there. So I could not attend the meeting. But we did not receive any particular guarantees against further harassment from Mr. Tupurkovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After these events at Petrinja -- let me rephrase this question and ask you one question before that. So was there any media coverage of the events in Petrinja, both in Croatian media or in other areas? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that. Yes, yes. Thank you. I know that television stations broadcast that terrible picture at Petrinja, because people, civilians tried to enter the barracks. Hundreds of people tried to enter the barracks, afraid of -- and some military personnel wanted to accommodate these people in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Whose barracks?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA barracks at Petrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Vasil Gasica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No. What was the name of the army? Please let us not overlap. Make a pause between answering. When you said the civilians were trying to find refuge in a barracks, you meant JNA barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will make sure that I do make a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was going on at Petrinja? Was it reflected in the everyday life of the ordinary people at Banija? What was the reaction of the people there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately it had major ramifications. From that day on, village guards started to be set up. Some people tried to sell their livestock to buy any kind of rifle. Village guards, village sentries started to be set up in all Serb-inhabited villages close to Petrinja and Sisak, Dvor Na Uni, Kostajnica, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there were attempts on the part of the Serbian population to acquire weapons. They would sell a cow to buy a rifle. Is it known to you what was the situation on the Croatian side? Let us -- let us call it that way, and I apologise for using that term. When it comes to arming, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is also a topic specifically on the list. Illegal arming of Croats; it's on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot understand how can such objection be raised. I'm not discussing an abstract topic. I'm talking about specific places, specific people, and about the witness, whether he knows anything about that or not. We are not dealing with politics. We are trying to establish facts. Facts in Kostajnica and around Kostajnica, and very briefly. These questions are very brief. Witness knows the names of villages, the names of people, knows the relevant period, and it would be very useful for all parties, the Bench and the two sides, parties, to know more about that and hear it from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I had not understood Your Honours to limit the subjects that it did not want to hear more evidence about to vague evidence about it. I'm happy to hear specific evidence that is going to "establish facts." I thought that the topic was the topic and Your Honours had heard enough about that topic, whether it's specific evidence or vague evidence or general evidence or what kind of evidence. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what do you submit now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would submit that it's on the list and therefore it should be -- we shouldn't go into it anymore. Unless Your Honours want to modify your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you done? Thank you. Objection upheld. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my respected friend from the Prosecution never objected when the witness was explaining how Serbs attempted to arm themselves. Now we are in an absurd situation. Is there any sense in leading evidence in these proceedings? Your instruction, the Bench's instruction, was referring to an attempt to streamline the proceedings and not to preclude examination of evidence. Your intention was to preclude evidence on general topics, but now we are dealing with a location of which we know nothing. We don't know who, when, what, at Dubica, at Cerovljani, et cetera. Although we did make reference to it one day when there were victims. The Prosecution alleges that there is a state of armed conflict throughout the relevant period in this area of RSK. So should we towards the end of the proceedings say that something has been sufficiently established? This would be pre-judging facts, Your Honours. I will, of course, strictly observe the guidelines of the Bench. I'm not repeating for the tenth time something, but we are dealing with specific events. This witness from Kostajnica is not testifying as to facts from Zagreb or Zadar. He is testifying as to the facts and events happening in his town, his village, and this is why he was summoned here. And this is what I'm trying to explain to the Chamber. I'm not trying to breach Your Honours' guidelines, and I'm not seeking exceptions that would favour the Defence or put us in a more favourable position than the Prosecution, but I'm using Your Honours' -- and how can I and whether I can perform my duties at all, if so constrained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the Bench has ruled on this matter. Extract facts, as you say, from the witness about Kostajnica, but refrain from illegal arming of the parties. Either side, whether the Croats or the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. Your Honour, I believe that we've reached the time for our break. So may I resume after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are very right, Mr. Milovancevic. We are going to take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, at the very beginning I omitted to ask you something that seems very logical. In the period 1990, 1991, 1992, where did you reside? Which place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I lived and worked in Sisak. I was a manager at Autopromet Sisak company. After that, war found me in the position in a personnel service of the steelworks of Sisak. I was manager of the legal department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Up to which point were you residing in Sisak? You said war found you in Sisak. Did you stay there? What happened?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this would be a lengthy story. I don't know whether the Bench will have the need to hear it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you tell us if you left Sisak, where did you leave to? If need be, I will ask you additional questions.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I left Sisak on the day when my children completed the first grade of elementary school. It was on the 15th of June, 1991. We left for Belgrade. Later I returned to Banija because my home village is 15 kilometres away from Sisak in the so-called Serbian part of Banija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mentioned that you left Sisak on the 15th of June, 1991, why did you do so? Was there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Given that I was a member of the SK movement for Yugoslavia, this was a political party which was populated by many military officers, and the -- may I say that the Socialist Party of Croatia, a Yugoslav-oriented party, the one I mentioned before, went into the SK because this was the last attempt to save and preserve Yugoslav -- Yugoslavdom and Yugoslavia. We were far more threatened in Croatia, we who advocated any form of Yugoslav or pro-Yugoslav orientation, far more in danger than others who favoured other options which unfortunately won the day. If you allow me to say one fact. The first explosive device was planted in the -- on the premises of the SK movement for Yugoslavia, a party headed by Ms. Jakolic who was a Croat and that party had its head in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To avoid interpreting your answers, could you explain what was your reason for leaving Sisak?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I was afraid I'd be liquidated, assassinated. Mr. Silvije Degen defended me before a Sisak court because I had been accused for organising meetings and rallies of the SK League of Communists-Movement for Yugoslavia. This is a known fact. It can be searched for in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to broach another subject, Witness, Mr. Dobrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt. I'm just wondering if -- just to assist in being able to follow the evidence, if Defence counsel wouldn't mind just asking when he returned from Belgrade to Banija, just a date, so that we can sort of follow what the -- how the evidence goes. If that wouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, that's a request to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is only logical, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Dobrijevic, that you up to the end of term you took your children to Belgrade. When and where to did you return?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I returned to Samarica on the 1st of August. I returned to Samarica, and there I tried to organise Territorial Defence of the Serbian villages that were left out of the municipality of Sisak and were annexed to the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we're talking about Kostajnica in 1991, could you tell us which events would be, in your opinion, the most important ones in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Kostajnica is a very interesting location geographically speaking for Banija, because neither of these municipalities had any access to Bosnia for supplies, Bosnia and Yugoslavia further, except for Kostajnica and Dvor Na Uni. However, Kostajnica is very close to the municipalities that I'm referring, and Dvor Na Uni is 100 kilometres long. It winds through a wooded area that we call Samarica. And upon -- on 26th of June, 1991, when Croatian paramilitaries made an incursion, the overall territory was cut off from any supplies or any other possibility to bring in any supplies to the population inhabiting that part of Banija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say, "We were cut off," could you specify which area was cut off, which municipalities and villages?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it will be useful for the Bench to know that the demarcation line followed the courses of the Sava and Kupa rivers. Everything was -- on the right bank of the Kupa River belong to these. But Kostajnica is on the bank of the Una River, and there were no other communications across the rivers apart from Kostajnica and Dvor Na Uni, and there was no possibilities to bring in supplies for the population from Bosnia and Yugoslavia other than those two places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I specify to the Bench a page in the atlas for easier reference. I opened the atlas on page 21, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you said when referring to Kostajnica that it borders Bosnia. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The largest municipality, the largest settlement in that area is Sisak. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sisak was the centre of the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On this map in the vicinity of Sisak there is south to it the municipality of Petrinja. One road goes from Sisak to Petrinja, and another goes towards Dubica. When you say that towns and villages were cut off, could you specify the area where these people were cut off upon the incursion of Croatian paramilitaries in the Banija region?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the settlements across the Sava River Sunja was one of the places controlled by Croatian forces and we could not reach Dubica on the road Sisak-Sunja-Dubica. That road was disrupted. So what I'm trying to say is that the only communication from Banija to gain access to Bosna and Yugoslavia took the Kostajnica direction or Dvor, but I said Dvor was 100 kilometres away and the road took the area of Samarica, very wooded area, so Kostajnica was the most logical and the closest means of communication. This is why Croatian paramilitaries made incursion into Kostajnica and President Tudjman had visited Kostajnica three days before the incursion to make sure that Serbia -- Serbs in Banija would be cut off from supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the entry of Croatian paramilitary forces into Kostajnica on the 26th of June, 1991. How did that occur?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Proof that Croatian forces could pass through such large territory controlled by the Serbs without any problems only that is proof, actually, that the Serbs neither wanted nor were ready to wage war, because forces from Zagreb passed through the Sisak-Sunja-Kostajnica area, that route, and the Petrinja-Kostajnica road, and from these two routes they entered Kostajnica under the slogan or the pretext that they were to attend the funeral of a man who had died in Zagreb. However, that was a pretty suspicious column, because the vehicles had different licence plates from all over Croatia so that people who were following this in a way realised that was in fact an occupation of Kostajnica which actually did happen overnight, because during the nights the reinforcements came in uniform - shall I say paramilitary forces from Zagreb - and already the next morning a raid in Kostajnica started. Check-points were set up throughout the town and on the exit and entry points so that no one could pass through Kostajnica without the vehicles passing through Kostajnica being searched and stopped for a thousand -- for umpteenth times, and that is when the Serbs started leaving Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this refers to the 26th of June, 1991, what you have just told us. Do you know what was the total of the forces that came in Kostajnica in the described way?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The answer -- the estimate was that at that time about 300 policemen arrived of the then still the Croatian para-army, but after three months when Kostajnica was liberated there were about 600 Croatian troops there, but they had another entry to Kostajnica which they used, that is from Novska through the Sukri Kamen [phoen], from Jasenovac along the Una River, and this is also the route which they took to withdraw from -- towards Novska and further on to Zagreb after Kostajnica had been liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And how did events then evolve further in Kostajnica? You say 300 people, armed people, came. What happened in July? Did anything happen in July?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were raids, and I should seek to restrict this answer to the maximum. These forces remained in Kostajnica for three months. The Serbs set up a Territorial Defence. The staff -- in charge of the staff was Branko Mitrovic who was also the president of the municipality after Mr. Miocevic had been replaced, and its seat was in the village of Komogovina, some 10 kilometres away. That is on Banija at the very exit from Kostajnica. So these forces stayed in Kostajnica for three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will suffice. Does the names of Glinska Greda, Trnjani, Cakale, Bestrma, do these village names ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had to defend Kostajnica, and it was liberated but this is a question that I wish to elaborate a bit on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Excuse me. We shall come to the issue of the deliberation of Kostajnica, but now we are just following a chronological order. That is what I'm looking for, a chronology of events. So I'm asking you about the 21st, 22nd of August, 1991, and please be brief, as brief as you can be. Why is this date important?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I cannot be very briefer in responding to this, but to use the time that this does require because this has -- concerns a bloody crime on Banija. Namely, between the 21st and the 22nd of August there was a bloody orgy in the area of these villages. My village Bestrma where I said I was born and a number of neighbouring villages. I did not mention this before because the learned Prosecutor did not allow me to speak about arming, but I will say that on the 10th of April, 1991, there arrived in Sisak 120 volunteers, primarily from the Argentine who are descendants of the former Ustashas who fled to Latin American countries via the rap channels, the rap canals. At that time in the yard of the police administration in Sisak which is -- abuts with the yard of the court in Sisak where I used to work, so in that yard there were a number of motor vehicles which they used to make armoured vehicles with which to attack these villages, and I believe that it is important --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Please talk about this particular date in brief. What happened on the 21st and on the 22nd? Who arrived where and what happened?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: In the early morning hours from the village of Komarevo, that area, and that is the neighbouring village adjacent to my own village Bestrma, which was a stronghold of the Ustashas in the Second World War, and Tudjman actually said that Komarevo was not defending Sisak or Zagreb but Komarevo was defending Europe in this war. So it was from that village that a column dressed in the uniforms of the Yugoslav army came, and they descended upon the first village of Madzari where two roads cross, one leads to the village of Glinska Greda and on to my own village of Bestrma and then the village of Kinjacka and Brdjani. So that is one column. The second column, convoy from the village of Trnjani -- rather, from the village of Madzari goes to the village of Trnjani, the village of Cakale, Velika Kinjacka, and this is where the two columns meet. Each of these columns in passing through these villages performed a bloody orgy. When they entered Glinska Greda, they called the population. So they were in uniforms of the Yugoslav army. They called the population to come out of their houses, and when the people started exiting their houses they mowed them down by bursts of fire killing Misa Vucinic, Ratko Djekic, who was a pensioner, Kragulj, whose first name I cannot remember. This guy was the only armed one because he was an armed sentry the village sentry. He was the only person with a weapon, and I cannot remember the name of the fourth person that was killed. However, I have brought for this august Tribunal a list of people -- of 611 people killed in Sisak, and I hope that you will allow me to speak about this later, because it is quite verifiable by whom and when all these people were liquidated. So this column then goes on to and enters my village Bestrma, liquidates in his own yard Dragan Biskupovic, a well-known musician who was otherwise a driver in the ironworks in Sisak. I am pointing this out because the criminals who killed him also castrated him because they recognised him. He was an exceptionally good man, if one can say that of a man. Later his wife was also killed in this war, and I wanted his son to come here and take the witness stand before the Tribunal at The Hague. Nedeljko Cajic, the father of two minor children was then killed, and this column is by now already descending to the Blinksi [phoen] road and towards the village of Mala Kinjacka. The second part of the column enters the village of Trnjani and kills Dragan, I think, Tatisic, and they kill a young girl -- well, I cannot remember her name either. You see how it is. But this was a 18-year-old girl. Her name was Zeljka. I cannot remember the surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it maybe Zeljka Vojinovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is Zeljka Vojinovic. She was on the window of her house, and she was killed by a neighbour from the village of Madzari who was in that column. In the village of Cakale, they killed Lazar Stanic, also a well known assemblyman of the Assembly -- Municipal Assembly of Sisak and the president of the local commune who, as the president of the village, sought to meet -- and this column, thinking that it was the Yugoslav army. So in the village of Kinjacka, Velika Kinjacka, Dragan Bekic, Pero Crljenica were killed on the road. Leposava Pajic was wounded, and Dragica Trlenica [phoen] too. And at the end of the Kinjacka village they killed Ranko Martinovic who was the only one who was armed, and he was under -- with a hunting rifle because he was standing guard. It was already daybreak by that time, and having met, combined these two columns go on towards Sunja to village of Brdjani. As day broke and it became light, the local sentries assembled and set up a barricade at the entrance to the village of Brdjani, and there there was a skirmish between the paramilitary of the Croatian side and the village guards, and four to five Croatians were killed, and now there is a monument which is -- was erected to these paramilitary, para-army members who actually committed this bloody orgy on the 21st and the 22nd. And I take this 21st to be the overt beginning of the war, at least in Banija, because after that event nothing was the same in Banija anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, allow me to say that the witness needs to slow his pace somewhat and he needs to come up for air sometimes and just do it so we can keep pace with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. The witness was obviously and manifestly excited when he was speaking. That is why I didn't interrupt him. But I let him go on at such length because of his assessment that that was what led to the outbreak of war in Banija and that is when the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So this was on the 21st and 22nd of August in 1991. Did I remember the date correctly?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why -- when and why was there an attempt to liberate Kostajnica? You said that Kostajnica is -- was liberated. First of all, tell me, why do you say it is the liberation of Kostajnica and when was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the paramilitary forces of Croatia stayed some three months in Kostajnica. In the meantime, a number of incidents occurred because those units from Kostajnica attacked our territorial guards. So that a young lad, for instance Bogdan Sarengaca, from the village of Velasnja [phoen] was killed and he was the only son in his family, the only child. And there was another guy who was killed, another lad. I cannot remember his name at -- right now. He was from a neighbouring village, I believe. I -- and perhaps his surname was Rokvic, but be that as it may, the two of them were killed. And the very difficult situation ensued, and the decision was taken that Kostajnica had to be liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a minute. Who, who decided that Kostajnica is to be liberated? What forces were to be employed for that? You are talking about the liberation of Kostajnica from whom?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Then at that time, except for the Territorial Defence -- so except for the Territorial Defence which comprised the domestic population, both urban and rural, armed and organised, so that the most renowned person was practically the commander of the village. So this is what we had in Banija. When Kostajnica is concerned, we had Branko Mitrovic who was the municipality president, and he was also the commander of the Territorial Defence. My unit in which I was one of the assistants in the staff was in this area towards Sisak, and the Sas, Zivaja, Kostajnica, Bacin, Banija triangle, plus the other villages, they were in this area starting from Novska. But the principal decision was adopted at the -- by the Territorial Defence Staff of Kostajnica. Kostajnica was liberated exclusively by its own citizens, its own people, without any policemen or territorial member from without, apart from the fact that there were some 20-odd lads from my unit who helped them, and one of these combatants from the Territorial Defence belonging to the Sisak municipality was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Territorial Defence unit was headed by the president of the municipality Ranko Mitrovic. In -- with regards to that, I'm going to ask you this: Didn't you answer my question in the previous session that after the first multi-party elections the president of the municipality was a Croat in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Miocevic was president of the municipality up to the moment when he proposed for a part of the municipal budget of Kostajnica be earmarked for the arming of Croatian paramilitary forces. Then Mr. Miocevic was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologise, Your Honours. I did not interrupt my witness in time while you were conferring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Dobrijevic, I'm going to ask you once again. You said that counsel are in the Municipal Assembly. Mr. Miocevic who was also the municipal president. When was he replaced? You mentioned the circumstances of that event. When and why?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the specific date, but he was replaced exclusively because he had proposed that a part of the municipal budget of Kostajnica be earmarked for -- and transferred to the military budget of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that other councillors in the Assembly did not accept that or was there another reason?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did not accept that. And given that Racan's party was victorious in the elections and that Racan performed a salto mortale and joined the policy of Franjo Tudjman, which can be corroborated by a slew of documents, Racan was, among other things, vice-Prime Minister. At that time, Municipal Assembly members started defecting into the SDS, Serbian Democratic Party, and councillors on the SDP ticket started going into the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Will I be mistaken if I conclude on the basis of what you said that on -- for these reasons president of the municipality in 1991 was Branko Mitrovic during the skirmishes that you explained?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is what you said?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when did the Territorial Defence units of Kostajnica enter Kostajnica? Was there any combat, and could you refresh our memory as to the number of Croatian paramilitaries in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: There was some 600 members of Croatian paramilitary units in Kostajnica at the time, but Kostajnica was very difficult to defend, you know, because it is surrounded by Serbian population from all sides, and the main line was the river of Una and there was a bridge for Bosanska Kostajnica. Maybe 26th of September combat started and then finished within one day. On the Serbian side there were six or seven killed, as far as I know. Somewhat less on the Croatian side because Croatian forces surrendered. The most -- majority of Croatian forces surrendered in Bosanska Kostajnica to the army of Yugoslavia, and 60 to 80 members of Croatian paramilitaries surrendered to the Territorial Defence unit on the hill that we call Djed above Kostajnica. Some of the forestry school deans from Zagreb was there. There was some people from Television Zagreb or Zagreb television station among these. I have video footage of the treatment of these captured members of the Croatian paramilitary, and I can tell you, as far as I know, there were not hurt after being captured. Not a hair on their head was dishevelled. You can see on that footage them, you know, lounging about, smoking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Kostajnica was liberated by Territorial Defence units in the way that you described, and they were under the command of Branko Mitrovic, municipal president. What was the ethnic composition of the Territorial Defence of Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this question. 111 fighters of the Territorial Defence were Croats. So 111 fighters on the side of the Territorial Defence that was liberating Kostajnica were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe if you permit me, may I continue? On the 1993 elections, first multi-party elections in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, 1.200 Croats in Kostajnica voted, which means that they must have been more than 2.000 of them staying there if we take into account those minors who had no vote at the time, which is proof that Croats were not expelled from Kostajnica. To the contrary. Most of the Croatian population of Kostajnica remained living there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm getting a little confused. I thought we were dealing with the ethnic composition of the Territorial Defence of Kostajnica. Was it composed of only 111 Croat fighters? Is that -- is that the entire constitution? I see now you're talking about voting. The next question deals with voting now. Let's exhaust one topic at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If it pleases the Bench, I will try to elicit an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it known to you, what was the number of Territorial Defence units of Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 500, 600 members. I don't believe there were more in Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you made reference to 111 members of the TO of Kostajnica and you referred to them as being Croats, does it mean that out of 500 or 600 that 111 were Croats? What you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly what you stated. In the Territorial Defence units of Kostajnica that were liberating Kostajnica, there were 111 fighters of Croat ethnicity. Inhabitants of Kostajnica and the surrounding villages who were the fighters of Territorial Defence of Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What ethnic group --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. To what ethnic group did the remainder belong? The question was what was the ethnic composition of the Territorial Defence. We still don't know to what group the remainder belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer that? Sir, you heard the question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The remainder were mostly Serbs. There were a few percentage points of others, Muslims or those who did not -- made any declarations as to their ethnicity. Most of them were of course Serbs, because Kostajnica used to be a Serb-dominated town in terms of population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You put the conflict in Kostajnica somewhere towards end of September 1991. You said, "As far as I can remember." Would mention of 12th or 13th of September, 1991, ring any bells or help you to connect that date with the battles around Kostajnica? May I ask you a direct question, because we have information about battles that took place on the 12th or 13th so that we do not have an impression that they were fighting over Kostajnica twice.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to Your Honours. So much time has elapsed and there are so many dates that I may be mistaken as to the correct date, and please tolerate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated that you captured a number of Croatian troops in Kostajnica. Were all of them captured or were there any who left Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Some of them left Kostajnica, as I said, in the direction of Novska --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- through Bacin, and some of them surrendered in Bosnia, Republic of Bosnia, because a regular Yugoslav army was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
