utterances.text: Thank you. At the time of that conflict and immediately after it, what happened to the population of Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Population of Kostajnica would go back to Kostajnica, which was only normal. A number of Croats, Croat inhabitants, left Kostajnica together with Croatian paramilitaries, but the largest part of the population stayed in Kostajnica. I'll corroborate that with the fact that at the subsequent elections in Republic of Serbian Krajina more than 1.200 Croats with the right to vote did take part in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say fighting around Kostajnica took one day. What happened to villages of Bacin, Dubica, and Cerovljani at the time? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: These are villages on the axis between Kostajnica and Novska, along the Una River in the so-called Banija triangle. As far as I know, there were some groups of Croatian paramilitaries there, and two or three days after the liberation of Kostajnica, an operation to liberate the rest of the villages along this axis was taken, the axis towards Novska, the aforementioned villages of Bacin and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it known to you personally that two or three days after the liberation of Kostajnica there were any skirmishes or there was now combat in those villages?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course there was some combat in those villages because there were strong groups stationed there, groups of Croatian paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After TO forces entered Kostajnica at Bacin, Dubica and Cerovljani, what happened to these villages next? Or did the troops, Territorial Defence troops, do they stay in these villages? Do they make further progress? This is the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The separation line between Republic of Serbian Krajina and Croatia is a very long one and a very unnatural one, so to speak, because it is meandering and that line had to be secured. The fighters who liberated the Kostajnica and the other villages, practically they manned the separation line to prevent Croatian paramilitaries from returning and retaking that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly, what area did this separation line go through.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot be very specific. I should have a map in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Apologise. We mentioned some major settlements in that area, Sisak, south of it Petrinja, then Kostajnica. You mentioned Sunja. With respect to these settlements, could you explain where the separation line went? We mentioned Dubica as well.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: From Sunja to Dubica and further towards Novska, that was the line of separation manned by the Kostajnica Territorial Defence in the area of separation between RSK and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From Sunja to Dubica and further to Novska this is how you described this line of separation. What does this term "line of separation" mean? What kind of a line is it? What it separates; who from whom?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Which means that we dug trenches, put in sentries. Sentries worked in shifts, and population was being secured from any incursions by any units from the other side. The Croats manned such a line towards us, and we had such a line towards them. It was fine when we had a natural boundary; for instance, the course of the River Sava or the River Una. But at places where no natural boundaries could be found, this line of separation went through fields, through forests and woods, and it was very difficult to man this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If on the basis of your answer I were to conclude this was a front line, would I be much mistaken?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: You wouldn't, no. You wouldn't be mistaken. You wouldn't be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since I do have a map, page 21, before me, how much kilometres are there between Sunja and Dubica approximately?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: 30, 35 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And so this line coincided with the front line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The front line was far longer, as I already explained. It wasn't a straight line. It was a line which coincided with some roads or natural features or barriers at -- in the -- on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that TO forces of Kostajnica, after entering Kostajnica, Dubica, Bacin, Cerovljani, manned this front line. Is it known to you that after these events, around mid-September 1991, there were any conflicts on that front line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: There were everyday conflicts of differing intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry. I'm just wondering if we could maybe establish briefly a basis for this line of questioning now, where the witness was at this time and how he knows these things. I don't think that's been established. It's not clear to me where exactly he was, except I think near Sisak, but it's not absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm grateful to my learned colleague Whiting for this remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Witness, you told us about many details regarding these name places. How do you know all this? Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Distinguished Mr. Prosecutor, it will be easy for you to understand, I believe. The villages of Sas up all the way to Zivaja, Crkveni Bok, Livanjski Bok, Strmen, these are all villages we're referring to, and these villages before the war used to be part of the Sisak municipality, and we bordered the municipality of Kostajnica, and in the village of Mala Gradusa we established a new municipality comprised of the remaining Serbian villages, 23 villages from the former municipality of Sisak which were left on this side of the border of RSK. I was one of the founders of that municipality, that's one thing; and the second thing I was deputy commander of the Territorial Defence in that area and we were adjacent to Kostajnica, our territory, that is, and we had joint actions and we made arrangements, and this was the only town that was in the radius of 15 kilometres from my headquarters. Another thing, commander of the Territorial Defence in that town was a young man from Kostajnica. I told you that 21 or 22 fighters from my unit took part in the liberation of Kostajnica. So I was in the immediate vicinity in all these actions and operations that were unfolding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. What happened in Kostajnica after the Territorial Defence units of Kostajnica entered the town? What happened in terms of functioning of the organs of authority and with the people in the area?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps this is not the right term to use when I say liberation of Kostajnica, because actually the same authorities that we had prior to the occupation of Kostajnica returned; namely, the president of the municipality with all his administration that was there, had been there before the occupation of Kostajnica. So in Kostajnica and in that portion of the Banija triangle there was not a single police station so that we attempted to establish organs of authority because government could not function immediately. There were houses that had been blown up and demolished. And of course, Your Honours, you know what it means when one enters a certain area, even though the authorities have been elected, but given the situation some time is required in order for such authorities to indeed start to properly and normally function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding the attitude of the authorities towards the domestic population, what was that like?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The very fact that such a large number of Croats remained in Kostajnica attests to the fact that the authorities were, shall I say, very acceptable. But then there were some other disruptive factors in -- at work, at work, and certain groups emerged. We could not even all them paramilitary units. These were some self-styled hooligans in different, all manner of uniforms, and they tried to establish their own government or authority, police or any other authority in different places. But I explicitly wish to stress that such occurrences had nothing whatsoever to do with the legal authorities in that part of Banija. And that was not only the case with Kostajnica. This was something which was the case with -- in the entire Krajina, but of course I'm testifying here only about the situation in the Banija area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You referred to the emergence of certain groups that attempted to organise themselves and to operate there, and you said that they were not the authorities. What did they do? How did they try to operate? Who were these people? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: This was violent behaviour on the part of individuals. There were certain groups -- there was one group, for instance, which was led by a person called Japan; I think he was killed. And another one was led by certain Stevo Borojevic, who I also believe was killed. There were different other smaller or larger groups who would terrorise the population at night. Not only Croats but also Serbs, but primarily the Croats, the Croat population. Until the police station was established in 1992, in the beginning of 1992, in January, we had lots of problems in Kostajnica with such self-styled groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about these problems, tell me how do you know about that. How do you know about these occurrences?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do know about it because I personally came to meet them. I knew them from the field there. And apart from that, I had very close communication with the president of the municipality, with the leadership, so that these were not unknown facts to me. And not only to me but to anyone there who was active in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a person Borojevic and a certain person by the name of Japan. Can you tell me, how were those people dressed? What did they represent? How did they introduce themselves? How did they act? You say they terrorised the population. Give me the specific fact.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: A very important fact is that these were frustrated people, frustrated chaps. There were a number of small groups and different groups. There was one judge in among them, and unfortunately some of them actually invoked Milan Martic's name saying that they practically constituted some sort of his police or army; whereas, in actual fact, they had never seen Milan Martic, or at least Milan Martic could not have even heard of them by that time. So that these were people who tried to project themselves as some sort of authority by invoking the name of the then most renowned person in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the authorities, what the Territorial Defence or, rather, whether they undertook any steps in order to prevent the operation of such groups?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, lots of steps were taken. I know of a case and with the leave of the -- Their Honours I will describe it. Namely, immediately after the liberation of Kostajnica, the Croatian population in that area was in jeopardy, precisely at the hands of these groups. And I know that some noted people from this area of the Banija triangle, Mr. Glavas, Mr. Misljenovic and a couple others, actually went to Knin and asked Milan Martic for help, for something, anything, to be done in order to prevent these and such developments that we had in the field. In order not to be asked by the distinguished Prosecutor again how I know that, let me say that it was very interesting that Milan Martic should appear in that portion of the Banija triangle at that time. I don't know whether he had been there any time before that. So he came by helicopter and held a meeting. He came two days later, and at that time there was a -- a unit of the Yugoslav army there which was under the command of the Banja Luka Corps at that time. I am underlining this because the Territorial Defence of Banija, its troops had nothing to do whatsoever vis-a-vis that unit, in terms of orders or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just want to ask you something in this connection. You mentioned a number of noted people who went to see Mr. Martic who then arrived two days later by helicopter. Why did they go to see precisely him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Because they thought him to be the man wielding the most authority in the Krajina then. And that was the reason which was also relayed to me later when I talked to those people who had been to Knin. They expected that Milan Martic would be able to take some steps, and they said, in regard of Mr. Borojevic -- and the commander of that brigade was commander Borojevic, Slobodan Borojevic, and the commander of this group was Stevo Borojevic. So we are talking about Slobodan Borojevic. I believe that at that time Mr. Martic simply issued an order and joined upon the commander Slobodan Borojevic to dismantle -- to remove from the bridge this group of self-styled camouflage people from the bridge towards Dubica and to have that manned by the military police, because I stress again we had no civilian police at that time in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just -- I just want to get a little more clarity on this. Mr. Martic wielded the most authority in the Krajina at that time. What kind of authority was this? Was he a minister or what kind of authority did he wield at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milan Martic at the time was the minister of the interior of the Krajina. However, in order to understand this genesis that I am developing here, at that time in that area there were no units of the Ministry of the Interior because the police had not been formed there yet, so that Milan Martic could not have had an information as to what was happening in the terrain, in the field there, because there were no police there. That is why Territorial Defence members and these other people who were Assembly men in the Municipal Assembly of Kostajnica actually went to seek assistance from Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Ministry of the Interior supervises the police, or does it supervise something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you say at the time he was the Minister of the Interior but there were no police formed yet, but you say he had authority. Over what did he have authority? Or over whom did he have authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Martic's authority was built very quickly, so to speak, because he was one of the people who aligned himself with the imperiled Krajina people, and irrespective of his function, he really had a charisma which was seen as charismatic in the Krajina. But Kostajnica had only been liberated a couple of days before this, and there had been no time for a police administration or a police station to be established there. Immediately after Milan Martic left, a month or so after that, a police station was set up in Kostajnica. Pero Vuruna was assigned its chief, and after that, probably on orders from Martic, he also established a police unit in the village of Sas, and that is because the situation there was volatile and there was the danger that the Croats could suffer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer, but you have not really been able to tell me over what or over whom he had authority. I take your point that you say he was a man of charisma, he had a lot of authority. Do I understand you by that to say - as you said, notwithstanding his functions - he had real power on anything? If he wanted things to happen, he could make them happen whether they were within his area of functioning or beyond. He was a man with effective and real power in the Krajina. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. You have understood me well. He did have authority in that area, too, but only subsequently when the police was established there. In this moment of anarchy, no one could have had authority there, actual authority. He wanted to establish his authority to protect the population, but the actual establishment was later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The actual establishment was later, but at this stage already before it was established he was exercising authority, real authority, let alone authority that comes from the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We are not talking about the authority in the sense of legal authorities. We are talking about his personal authority, authority as a person. So such a personal authority was required to change the situation in the field rather than just observe it and register it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't hear my question very well. That was exactly what I was saying. That personally as a human being he just had this authority, this charisma that you're talking about, and even before he was established he was able to exercise his authority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And he could get things done. And you say that he managed to get this police station established in these two villages. Thank you very much. I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You referred to another Borojevic, the commander of the unit and his conduct in connection with these developments. Why did you mention him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I referred to Slobodan Borojevic. He was the commander of the brigade which was comprised within the command of the Banja Luka Corps, was under the command of the Banja Luka Corps. Precisely owing to such relations in the field and the emergence of these different self-styled groups and because of the jeopardy they posed to the population, that man tried to leave or, rather, he threatened that he would leave the area with his unit unless something changed there. And in my book or -- not according to me but according to claims made by these people who went to seek assistance from Milan Martic, that was one of the principal reasons; namely, to prevent Slobodan Borojevic and his regular unit from leaving the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the position of Mr. Martic had been towards the action of such groups and individuals?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Both then and later when I spent a short while as a more close associate of Mr. Martic's, I know that he absolutely condemned such conduct, and not in a single occasion did he tolerate any self-styled groups or any kind of conduct which would be in contravention of discipline and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now take a look at -- on our monitors. Exhibit marked 602, which is a 65 ter Prosecution list document, and it is an order by Mr. Martic referring to the municipality of Kostajnica of the 26th of November, 1991. You see a document in front of you. In the top left-hand corner it says the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, the Ministry of the Interior, Knin, the 26th of November, 1991. Do you see that, Mr. Dobrijevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll up so as to be able to see items 1 to 4 of this text. Thank you. I shall read for you items 1 and 4 of this. 1 says: "In accordance with the written and oral agreement with the commander of the Banja Luka Corps, Lieutenant General Nikola Uzelac, for civilian authority affairs in war conditions, in the area of Dubica of the Municipal Assembly of Kostajnica, up until the establishment of a regular police station of public security in Dubica, all work and duties of public security in the local commune of Dubica shall be discharged by the Kostajnica public security station with assistance from the military police from the Banja Luka Corps, i.e., the 3rd Detachment (with commander Captain First Class Slobodan Borojevic)." Item 4 reads: "All persons wearing camouflage uniforms but not members of the SAO Krajina Police, not holding appropriate authorised IDs or have not been legally assigned according to a decision of the Ministry of the Interior of the Krajina shall return their markings, police patches, and report to the military department of Kostajnica in order to be assigned to the war units of the Yugoslav People's Army." Did you see this, Mr. Dobrijevic? The signature in the bottom right-hand corner is Milan Martic. Actually, it is typed out. And there is a seal. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described in situation in Kostajnica and the surrounding area. Does this order correspond to your knowledge about what was going on in the field at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: This order confirms what I was telling you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question before we take the break. In item 4 of this order, there is reference to persons wearing camouflage uniforms but who do not have any official IDs, any documents authorising them to do so, and nor are they members of Krajina police. Is it known to you that there were such people out in the field who were purported to be policemen or -- or representatives of authorities at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly what I said. There were various groups self-styled roaming the area before official police authority and hierarchy was established. Some were imprisoned, some perished in intergroup recriminations and fightings, and some had to be -- had to enter the legal formations of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When was SAO Krajina Police established, and this time in terms of its being fully fledged?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, Kostajnica in January, then Gradusa, Petrinja, Glina. This is the period when Krajina police started functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this would be the right time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you very much. We'll take the break and come back at a quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one small housekeeping lest it slips through the cracks. The Trial Chamber has an oral decision to render on a number of motions and submissions that have been placed before the Chamber, and I'll go on to read the decision. You will be given copies of this, so you don't need to write. The Trial Chamber is seized of several motions and submissions in relation to the military expert report of Milisav Sekulic. The Trial Chamber has considered all of the arguments of the parties and in the interests of justice and of a fair and expeditious trial will render an oral decision today. A written decision addressing all the issues raised and elaborating the reasoning of the Trial Chamber will be rendered on Monday, the 13th of November, 2006. Having requested the curriculum vitae of Milisav Sekulic which was provided to it today, the Trial Chamber has found that Milisav Sekulic meets the requirements for being considered a military expert relating to the issues in dispute in this case. However, before addressing Milisav Sekulic's report under Rule 94 bis, the Trial Chamber notes the Defence's request for an extension of time to comply with the Trial Chamber's order of the 7th November 2006 and the Prosecution's objections thereto. The Trial Chamber further notes that this is not the first time that the Defence, in failing to meet a set deadline, requests a last-minute enlargement of time which should appropriately have been requested at a much earlier stage. The Trial Chamber finds that such behaviour is far below the requirement professional standard of counsel before this Tribunal. The Defence's request for extension is denied. However, it should be said that the Defence, in failing to meet the deadline set, has forfeited the opportunity granted to it by the Trial Chamber to provide adequate references for this report. Turning now to the report itself. The Trial Chamber has assessed the report in light of the Rules and the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. As a result of this evaluation, the Trial Chamber has found that in order to be able to admit the report as an expert report it is necessary to redact it. The Trial Chamber also grants the Prosecution request for cross-examination. The Trial Chamber has redacted the report and admits it into evidence. May the registrar please give this an exhibit number. The redacted version will now be distributed to the parties, and this redacted version will be appended to the written decision. Thank you very much. The witness may come in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Exhibit number will be 1012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Dobrijevic. There was a little matter that needed to be attended to. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I utter a single sentence by your leave? We've heard your oral decision. The opinion of the Chamber with regard to our attitude to deadlines fell very heavily on us, so we had to do the expert witness's job to reconcile hundreds of footnotes, and we are nearing the end of these proceedings. So we never intended or we never acted in bad faith or disregarded Chambers's orders. Objective circumstances were at play. Justified or not justified, this will be for you to judge, but let it be noted that our attitude toward your orders is as responsible as possible under the circumstances surrounding this Defence team. This is the only thing I wanted to say with regard to that. And if you allow me, I would like to continue examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I hope you understand that the Chamber also said that with a very heavy heart. Okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, before the recess the last thing that we dwelled upon was the period when in the area of Banija there was established and started functioning the SUP. Do you recall that period?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You remember discussing that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the very beginning of your statement you said that you were for a while a coordinator for the SUP for Banija. When was that? Who appointed you, and what were your duties and tasks? As brief as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that my role or my post was not that important. However, Mr. Milan Martic, as the then minister of police of Krajina, simply judged that a person of my qualities ought to help him at least in terms of information when it came to relations obtaining in the area of Banija. This was for a brief period, three, three and a half months. I do have in my personal archives the decision on my dismissal. I was appointed in December 1992, and in mid-April 1993 I was removed from that position, and I was ordered at the same time to try to set up a military court with the help of the Minister of Defence. I cannot recall his name. I will. It will come back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This will suffice. With regard to this situation and the circumstances obtaining in the area of municipalities of Kostajnica and the town of Kostajnica and the towns of Dubica, Bacin, Cerovljani, Zivaja and Sas, and we are dealing with the September, October, and November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which state existed as an internationally recognised entity? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Exclusively the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the then minister of interior of the federal state. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It was General Petar Gracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Out on the ground in any of the republics of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, who was responsible for organising the Ministry of Interior? Who was in charge of the federal level, and who was in charge of republican level?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the federal secretary, federal police, and then republican police authorities as subordinated level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question pertaining to Kostajnica and the surrounding settlements. In whose military zone of responsibilities these settlements were in? Is it known to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've reiterated that. That was within the area of responsibility of the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your CV that we referred -- made reference to at the very beginning, you said that you were a minister in the government of Mr. Babic in mid-1995. Could you tell us when was that government premiered by Mr. Babic, when was it elected, at least a month, and which portfolio did you hold?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: That government as is known was elected in Topusko. I believe it was on the 27th or 28th of July, 1995. That was the government with the shortest term of all governments because it was established seven days prior to Operation Storm. I was a minister without portfolio in that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give us a date when it ceased being a government of Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very difficult to tell when it ceased to be Babic's government, given that that government still today --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Milan Babic, as Prime Minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, was elected toward the end of July 1995 and that you were a minister in that cabinet. Is it known to you anything about the departure of Mr. Babic to Belgrade on the 2nd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to seek leave from the Chamber to elaborate upon - very briefly - on the handful of days of the existence of this government before the police action Operation Storm. Upon the election of the government, we had received intelligence by the -- Mile Mrksic, the then chief commander of the RSK that Krajina had been attacked, and the whole of the government set off from Topusko to Knin to attend a government session, and in Knin this government issued certain conclusions because attacks against the Krajina had already started in the peripheral areas. Among other decisions, another decision was taken that five ministers and Prime Minister Babic should depart for Belgrade because the late Prime Minister Milan Babic had an appointment with the US ambassador Peter Galbraith in Zagreb, and the other ministers were there to help organise the affairs that -- and performance of the functions that we had as members of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for this interruption. Who was the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Pursuant to this decision of the Knin session of the government, did you go to Belgrade? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We set out to -- for Belgrade early in the morning. In Belgrade there was quite a lot of activity. We made great efforts to inform not only the Yugoslav and Serbian leaderships but also ambassadors of other countries. I remember I drew a letter to Kofi Annan. I don't know who else was in charge of drafting letters addressed to important international factors to prevent an imminent attack against the Krajina. Mr. Babic, on the 2nd of August, went for talks with Peter Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for doing this to you. On the 2nd of August of which year did Mr. Babic go to meet Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd of August, 1995, three days before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please state it for the record. 2nd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this chronology is clear. I'd like to reiterate it. I was one of the ministers who was tasked with attending that meeting, but at the last moment Prime Minister Milan Babic decided to hold talks with Peter Galbraith on his own, and as far as I know that meeting lasted from at least 8.00 p.m. to 11.00 p.m. And Mr. Babic returned from that conversation. He was quite excited, and he reported the ministers present there; Svetozar Vincic [phoen], Minister of Finance, and Mile Bosnjic, Minister of Trade. I was there, and other people who worked in the government's representative office at Terazije in Belgrade. And Milan Babic reported back to us the following: Peter Galbraith put it this way, President Tudjman has 1.000 troops on the border, 100.000 in reserve, and he definitely is going to attack the Krajina. Therefore, the only chance to save or to stave off an attack against Krajina is for the delegation that was then in Geneva, meaning Lazar Macura, Minister of Foreign Affairs Mile Vojinovic, assistant to Mr. Martic at that time Mr. Prijic, and former commander of the army General Mile Novakovic, and that was the delegation in Geneva at the time. We were requested to deploy all possible means and to prevail upon through our authority of this delegation to accept whatever may be requested of it in order to prevent war. Failing that, and I'm quoting verbatim the records of the late Prime Minister Babic as follows: Peter Galbraith had said that if this is not going to be accepted, there will be nobody we could seek help from. Yugoslavia was prevented from helping us, apart from issuing appeals to the international community. And even if Yugoslavia were to be engaged in war, it had fuel just for 15 days of operations. And I'm talking about fuel to conduct a war. These words were uttered by Mr. Milan Babic when relating the talks he had with Peter Galbraith that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm sorry, Mr. Dobrijevic. You may have mentioned this. I may have missed this. What ministry were you a minister of at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Minister without portfolio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We failed to register that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you sought to establish contact with the Republika Srpska delegation in Geneva. Did you indeed get in touch with them and what was achieved?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we communicated with that delegation throughout that night, and I have to admit that not even the delegation was united initially in the sense that everything should be accepted, but of course these details are not crucial for this august Tribunal, but we agreed that whatever our delegation was requested should be accepted, and as far as I know, it was agreed that the negotiations would continue on the next Thursday at the Pleso airport in Zagreb at a high level, meaning the Prime Minister and the ministers, that the railway would be unblocked, and that we were to deal with and resolve economic and military issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was -- did the delegation of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Geneva accept that, and what happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely the delegation fully accepted this, and in fact in a way we tried to have a modest celebration of that on the premises. However, unfortunately nevertheless the republic of the Serbian Krajina was attacked, and that morning I set off and went to Banja Luka because the present ministers had proposed me to be the coordinator of the refugee column. However, we expected that this would only -- that would only be the wounded, the elderly, and the children. However, the Storm operation had been so vehement that it actually marked the end of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the Republic of the Serbian Krajina could have defended itself on its own militarily from the attack by Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honours, I should like to explain this. After the Flash operation, after the collapse of Western Slavonia, I had a conversation with the late President Slobodan Milosevic. Two days after the fall of Western Slovenia, these are the words which I addressed to Slobodan Milosevic. I said to him, "Mr. President, the way that Western Slovenia has fared, that is how the entire Krajina shall fare should we be attacked by Croatia and that, for a basic reason, the reason being that there are not 50 or 60.000 combatants in the Krajina as some would have us believe. This is an army that has not been lined up for years. These are exhausted people, people exhausted from manning the demarcation lines and the front lines. There is not the slimmest of chances that they will be able to withstand an onslaught by the Croatian army, Croatian army which have 36 planes at the end of the war."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Milosevic say to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic literally said this to me, and since many conversations have been intercepted I would like to quote. He said verbatim: "Mr. Dobrijevic, you are under United Nations protection. If the United Nations do not save and protect you and you yourself are unable to fight and defend yourselves, what I can promise you is only that I will be building you houses in Serbia." And that was the end of the conversation between me and the late President Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'd like to pose a question, Mr. Milovancevic. Who had told you that there were 50 to 60.000 combatants in the Krajina? You said, "as some would have you believe." Who led you to that belief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never believed that, because I knew what the actual situation was. That was the number of combatants that we did have in the Krajina, but these were not people who were combat able. They were elderly people. There were elderly people with hunting rifles among them. And over the four years of the existence of the republic of the Serbian Krajina, many of those people had gone elsewhere to foreign countries in search of bread because of economic considerations. So that there could be no talk about any serious combat units that would be able to actually take on the Croatian army. We could not count on any such units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dobrijevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't think Mr. Dobrijevic answered the question. The question was: Who made you believe in any case, whether you believed it or not? Who had said that you had 50 to 60.000 combatants in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is the figure that was being bandied about in view of the fact that the population of the Krajina at that time numbered some 230.000. So it was a ratio. According to that population number, the number of able-bodied people capable of going to war would be about 50 to 60.000 people. But of course you know the Krajina stretches from Beli Manastir to Drnis. This is so long a border that, quite simply, even if we had such numbers in units prepared adequately for combat, they would have been unable to defend themselves from Croatia. But in my personal estimate, 25 to 30.000 soldiers were in fact actually capable of fighting at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Serbian delegation in Geneva accepted the agreement and then Croatia attacked on the following day. Do you know what President Milosevic mentioned to you happened; namely, did the United Nations defend Krajina then as it was under their protection, its protection?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a notorious fact. Had the United Nations indeed protected the Krajina, the Krajina would have survived. We were a UN protected zone, but at least in my view Croatia did not attack the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. Croatia attack the United Nations. And I believe that this is a fact that neither this Tribunal, this august Tribunal, or anyone in the world could -- can overlook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with a personal particular that you referred to, namely that at a certain point in time you had left Sisak, and in responding to a question of mine you said, "I left in order not to be killed." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what you meant by those words? What period does that refer to, and who would have killed you, Mr. Dobrijevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I really, really implore the -- Their Honours to allow me a couple of sentences relevant to -- related to the crimes in Sisak. In Sisak, 611 people were liquidated. I have that list. I have brought it with me, and I insist and I beg that that list be admitted as an exhibit into the case file before this Tribunal. 611 people were killed in Sisak, from which number 99 per cent were civilians. The liquidations in Sisak and -- were such -- Sisak is virtually what Jasenovac was in Croatia. Everything which happened around Osijek and Gospic was nothing compared to what was happening in Sisak. And allow me -- I just said this by way of introduction, as an initial premise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I asked you a very specific question and you are answering at some length. Who killed whom and why? Tell us in two sentences.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It was towards the end of 1990 and the beginning of 1991 that the liquidations in Sisak started. The list which I have contains the names, the last names, the time of liquidation, and in respect of certain individuals and persons also the place where the liquidations took place. One of the first liquidations was the murder of Mr. Damjan Zilic who was taken from his workplace in the refinery and his wife Mrs. Zilic Gligorincic [phoen] was a Croat and the president of the Petrinja municipality prior to the war. Many policemen were also killed, policemen who did not accept the new Croatian emblems, the so-called chequer-boards. In addition to that, the most liquidations in Sisak were of pensioners in the area of Zeleni Breg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Of what ethnicity were the killed people?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking solely about killed Serbs. Perhaps five or six people of Croat ethnicity are on this list and they were also liquidated. But the majority, not to say almost all of them, practically were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, we must finish. You must finish with this witness today for your examination-in-chief. We've taken too long to get your answers -- your questions answered. The question that you asked the witness specifically, and he can say that in one or two words, who was going to kill him. That was the question. And now he's telling us about the death of Mr. Damjan Zilic. That's all very interesting, but it doesn't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just a brief remark. I will be concluding in a very short time, perhaps five minutes, my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, I asked you who were you threatened by? Why did you want to, why did you have to leave Sisak?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: By your leave, Your Honours, let me just explain that Djuro Brodarac, two years before the establishment of the Croatian state who had been a famous Croatian nationalist and a commander of Croatian youth brigades during the Croatian maspok movement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just who was threatening to kill you. I think it's a very simple question. We understand that historical background, but just answer directly the question of the lawyer. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will do my best to lead the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, we have to abide by procedure here which is applicable before this Tribunal. I asked you a specific question. You described the situation, but please tell us who threatened you? Where does this danger threatening you - as you say mortal danger - come from?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Primarily from the MUP of Sisak. If that is sufficient, and I believe it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It is sufficient. Thank you. Can we now take a look at a Defence document on the monitor, 1D0134. Mr. Dobrijevic, there you have a human rights document, Human Rights Watch document before you from September 2006. I will read the second paragraph. It reads: "Between 1991 and 1992, more than 100 Croatian Serbs reportedly 'disappeared' or were killed in and around the town of Sisak, located about 50 kilometres south-east of Zagreb. They were victims of a campaign of killings and disappearances as well as of assaults and threats. In several cases, the suspected perpetrators were members of the Croatian army or police forces." Do these -- does this information by Human Rights Watch correspond to what you know from 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It will suffice. We have to bear in mind the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I propose that this document be admitted into the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection, though it's not Human Rights Watch. It's Amnesty International. But I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. You do admit that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this becomes Exhibit number 1013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see another document, which is Defence document 133. This is an Amnesty International document. It is page 13 that we're interested in. That's the English text version, page 13. And this document is dated 13 December 2004. I think that we have page 12 on the monitor. And this is the page, page 13 that we want to see. Can we have the entire page shown, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read a part of the text, Mr. Dobrijevic, from this page. "Information on crimes against the Croatian Serb population in and around Sisak, a town in central Croatia, situated approximately 50 kilometres south-east of Zagreb, became available in the early phase of the armed conflict. In several cases, the suspected perpetrators were members of the Croatian army or police forces. Between 1991 and 1992 Croatian Serbs in Sisak and in the surrounding areas became victims of a campaign of killings, abductions, 'disappearances,' assaults and threats. In November 1991, Amnesty International reported that up to 21 Serbian villagers are said to have been killed on 22nd August 1991 in the villages of Kinjacka, Cakale and Trnjani near Sisak when Croatian forces undertook a house-to-house search for Serbian paramilitaries who had fired mortars at the town of Sisak." And this was in quotation marks. "In a report published in March 1992, Amnesty International provided information on the killing of 12 Croatian Serbs in Sisak, some of whom had been employed in the INA oil refinery." And just a part of the next paragraph. "The crimes committed in Sisak relatively little known outside of Croatia were chosen as illustrative examples of a widespread pattern of violations committed against the civilian population allegedly by members of the Croatian army and police forces. To Amnesty International's knowledge, in no cases have these crimes been -- sorry. The crime of intimidation against Croatian Serbs and in general those suspected of not supporting Croatian independence which was prevailing in Sisak already at the start of the conflict is illustrated by the publication on 29 June 1991 in the Croatian magazine Slobodni Tjednik of a list of 14 Sisak residents. The list included the names and, in some cases, the addresses and telephone numbers of alleged enemy collaborators and members of the Yugoslav military intelligence, the KOS." This information produced by Amnesty International in 2004, does this correspond to the situation you attempted to describe and indeed described before this Tribunal today?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this is just minor information, and I should like to ask Their Honours to allow me at least a couple of minutes to elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, thank you. It is sufficient. We have to abide by procedure. The next question I'd like to put to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document as Defence Exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 1014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that at a certain point you were a member of a political party whose headquarters was blown up. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the title of the party?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: League of Communists-Movement for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the Croatian authorities of the ruling party towards that political party at that time in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: What was irritating Croatian authorities most at the time was any political party of Yugoslav provenance, of Yugoslav orientation. At the time, Croatian authorities wanted to turn the SDS into an extremist political party so as to be a counterweight of the then ruling Croatian extremist parties to provide justification for the then secessionists' endeavours of the Croatian leadership. I was part of the left, and whoever on the left tried to preserve Yugoslavia we were targeted, as such, by Croatian politics and Croatian forces of coercion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to that, one question. How do you explain your thesis that Croatian authorities in Croatian politics were against a political party which favoured Yugoslav orientation in a situation where Croatia insisted that its representative be president of Yugoslavia in 1991? And I'm referring to President Mesic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Stipe Mesic practically used his position to finish off Yugoslavia, and this is -- there is a well-known statement of his. "I've done my job. Yugoslavia is no more." I've brought this footage with me, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Dobrijevic. This is sufficient. And now the last exhibit, last document before I finish. Exhibit 1D0181. Before the document appears on the screen, I would like to explain that this is the minutes of the meeting of the Supreme State Council on the 12th of November, 1991. You can see before you a page of that -- those minutes. It states here, beginning at 12.15, chaired by president Dr. Franjo Tudjman, president of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. Do we have an English version, or maybe did I get the wrong thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had this translated a long time ago. There should be an English version in the system. I have a hard copy with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It has come up. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the first page in the B/C/S version to be scrolled down so that we can see the entire text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So, this would be a transcript of a meeting of the 36th Session of the Supreme State Council, 12th of November, 1991, chaired by President Tudjman. On the first page, below the word "president," it states that the president has introduced the agenda, and there is references to the attitude towards the Presidency of federal Yugoslavia. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let us take a look the page 114 in the B/C/S version of these minutes. In the English version that will be page 2. This text begins towards the bottom of the page, the one that I'm going to highlight for you. And I'm highlighting the words of Mr. Mesic. Mr. Mesic, at this meeting of the Croatian leadership, says the following: "Can I say something, because I have some other informations that will certainly be of interest to you." This is what he says at the beginning of the first paragraph, and I'm going to skip some text to speed up the proceedings. And somewhere else he says: "Through a contact from Korcula, I obtained a possibility to meet with Andreotti. That wasn't a firm commitment in my opinion, and being afraid of being compromised, I took the decision, whatever may happen. Not because this was a contact from Korcula but --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to object, and I waited for a moment because I wasn't exactly sure. I received notice that this document was going to be used just minutes before the session today, so I really have not had a chance to fully read it. But from the little I've read and from where things are going now, I object on grounds of relevance. That's the first objection. I don't see -- this I think is about -- going to be about the dissolution of Yugoslavia, one of the topics that Your Honour said you don't need more evidence about, about the Carrington negotiations, the Vance Plan negotiations and so forth. I think that's what this is about. Secondly, I would object on the grounds of -- of foundation. I'm not sure how this witness has any basis to talk about these -- this meeting and this transcript and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this topic is not dissolution of Yugoslavia. I -- we disagree with the learned friend. It didn't go for dissolution but the break-up of Yugoslavia, and this document testifies to the attitude of the then president of the Presidency, the Croat representative Stipe Mesic, as the president of the Presidency of SFRY. We had occasion to see a video footage of his famous sentence, and we had to ascertain what he said, whether he said it, and what he meant, and to understand that video footage it is necessary to take a look at this transcript of the minutes from that meeting, and many things will become clear once we've had a chance to see this part of the text. And the witness provided grounds for this exhibit to be led. The witness said Stipe Mesic came from Croatia to Yugoslav Presidency to break up that country, and he quoted Stipe Mesic as saying, "I've done my job. Yugoslavia is no more." So both grounds for this objection are not founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just note, I'm sorry, the date of this document is the 12th of November, 1991, and I don't believe that Mr. Mesic is the president of the Presidency on that date. I think he -- so I think it's inaccurate to say that this is when he's the president of the Presidency. And in any event, I think it's still an irrelevant topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you're on your feet, Mr. Milovancevic, and answering the point that has been raised, can you answer the other ground of objection that was raised earlier; namely, relevance. Or, rather, exclusion by the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, I believe that this issue has not been excluded by the Bench, and this is why I think it has not: We saw video footage recorded on the 5th of December when President Mesic speaks to the parliament in Zagreb, and he says, "I think that I've done my job. Yugoslavia is no more," followed by an applause. This was one month after this event, and this document is closely connected to the decisions of the Badinter Commission, and the Prosecution has led the conclusions of that commission on the borders of the then republics and the status of these republics. He's led it and drew some conclusions on the basis of that. And by leading this document we are connecting it with the Badinter Commission, and we give the Bench an opportunity to see what the Badinter Commission was doing. This document precedes the conclusions of the Badinter Commission and it contains very interesting facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I agree 100 per cent with you, Mr. Milovancevic, that we saw footage here of a video showing Mr. Stipe Mesic say those words. However, that was before the oral order of the Chamber, say, excluding certain topics. Now, as I sit here, I have no clear recollection that this topic was excluded or not excluded. Mr. Whiting says it was. You say it wasn't, but you justify that by saying the Prosecution led evidence on this. Obviously the things that were excluded, lots of evidence had been led on them. The reason they are excluded is because the Bench says it has heard enough, and I am saying, yes, when this video footage was played it was before that order, and since that footage the order has come out to say the Bench has heard enough. So you're going to have to establish by -- by reference to the order that this has not been excluded, not because it was led. We don't dispute that evidence was led on the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Defence will accept the stance of our learned colleagues that this would be superfluous if he were to accept that our thesis that Croatia was performing a violent secession from Yugoslavia. And this is issue number one, top issue in this trial, in this case. If the Prosecution were to utter that, then there's no job for us. And as to the question whether enough evidence has been led concerning this issue is an issue requiring consideration, very deep consideration. We've led examination through cross-examination of witnesses and some other documents, but now we have documents coming and originating from Croatian leadership itself. So this goes for a document where Croatian representative in Yugoslavia leadership precisely states what he'd been doing and what others had been doing very briefly and succinctly, and our learned colleague, during witnesses sitting here, pleads in the indictment something completely else, and we have no other evidence, no other exhibits, and no documents, and no other questions except for that one, Your Honours, for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I press my objection on both grounds, but I don't have any further argument about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: May I ask a question. Maybe Mr. Milovancevic can answer, but Mr. Whiting, maybe you could answer equally. Is this the first time that the Defence would be leading evidence of this nature on this area, or has there been other evidence coming from the Defence in respect of the subject matter in issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I would -- I would -- I think those are two different questions, and the answer to the first question, evidence of this nature it's probably the first time. I don't think we have any other transcripts of conversations from Croatian leaders, to my recollection. So I think evidence of this nature probably the first time. Is it the first time they've led evidence on this issue? Certainly not. This issue has been revisited again and again and again and again that Croatia was violently seceding from -- and not only has there been enormous amounts of evidence about that, but I really am not sure I see the relevance of even that claim to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, if I may just -- perhaps just help Judge Nosworthy also remember, that at some stage during the Defence case there was a dispute as to what the words of Mr. Mesic were actually, and the Defence played us footage - what do you call it, a clip - where his words were -- we heard him speak. So, yes, this topic has been visited before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, apologise. It is very difficult for me to agree with this statement. We haven't dealt with this issue in this manner. My learned friend from the Prosecution said something that really surprised me. Why would this be relevant? Protocol II to the 1949 Geneva Conventions in Article 1, paragraph 2, states that armed insurgency as opposed to civil war is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the state where this insurgence takes place and that state may suppress this insurgence by all means. And this is an issue that this Bench will have to take into careful consideration. This is an international law provision. Article 3 to Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions, and that protocol was adopted in 1977. Additional Protocol II Geneva Conventions. Article 3 says that civil war in a country in no way -- I'm paraphrasing Article 3 of Protocol II. Civil war in no way can be used for illegal actions against a high-contracting party, a sovereign state, and this referred to Yugoslavia. On the 12th of November, 1991, is a moment when Yugoslavia existed, Your Honours, and when its president Stjepan Mesic was doing something which ought to be of interest for this Bench, and we haven't led any evidence on this. What some politician briefly stated to the press, that's something which is in a newspaper article, but you're not going to base your decisions on newspaper articles. But this is a transcript of a meeting of the Croatian leadership which concerns the topic discussed by Article 3 of Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions. I'm very flabbergasted, Your Honours, why the Prosecution says that whether this is relevant or not. What have we been doing for the past 10 months? This indictment alleges an armed conflict within a republic in Yugoslavia. The fact that the ICTY refers to Yugoslavia means that it refers to a state, and now the Prosecution will preclude me from leading evidence on grounds that the Bench has ruled excluded some issues. But it cannot rule so. I -- my thesis is that this topic has only been superciliously, superfluously touched upon, and it's going to be the subject matter of a much deeper and comprehensive analysis of our expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, thank you for the long thesis and the scholarly address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just one minute, Judge, before you proceed. At the penultimate line of what you had said, did you mean superfluously or superficially, because it's relevant to what ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for the question. I said superficially, very little, in a very modest measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Having thanked you for all that long scholarly address, can I just find out something? You jumped after I'd spoken. Am I wrong to say the Defence played a clip of Mr. Mesic speaking in a -- to clear the point on what his actual words were? I'm wrong to say so? Because you said -- you started off by saying you cannot agree with what I was saying, and all I said was we have to remind Judge Nosworthy we had a clip here played in which -- which was produced by the Defence in which Mr. Mesic spoke, and you played that clip because there was a dispute as to what his actual words were. Now, and if playing that clip and the evidence that was led around that point was not dealing with this topic, I'm quite prepared to say -- to apologise if you say I'm wrong, sir. Was I wrong to say so? Is that why you disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Perhaps I spoke ahead of my own self. You did refer to that film, to that footage, to that clip. It was played, and we actually verified what was said in the footage. What I wanted to say is something else, that by seeing that video footage we did not actually deal with this topic comprehensively. I thought that your explanation had to do with the Prosecutor's objection, but I went farther than that. I was dealing with the nature of the objection, not with what you had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mine had to do with reminding Judge Nosworthy further that the topic had been dealt with, that's all. Whether it was in detail or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I read you. That is the way I understood, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the Bench would like to rule on the objection, and I think simply because this is the first time that we're getting this kind of testimony I am going to allow Mr. Milovancevic to proceed, this kind of minute from the Croatian authorities. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, I have read -- I have started to read for you the text marked in the B/C/S, 114, in which Mr. Mesic said that via a private Korcula link he had gone to Italy to visit Andreotti. And then he says: "I think it was good that I was there. Andreotti asked for some information which are now surprising for him." And I am skipping over. I'm going to the next paragraph, and I'm reading the continuation of the text. That ought to be on, for Your Honours -- let me just see what page it is. Page 16 of the translation. So Mr. Mesic says he had visited Andreotti, and he goes on to say: "But what is the most important for us?" This is what he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The translation has only --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 16 in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The English only has up to 12 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think what he means is it's -- it's page 16 on the bottom of the page, that the -- these are -- the English translation is -- it skips pages. It's excerpts. It's not a complete translation, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are with you now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We -- I'm sorry. We are with you now, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the English booth has the B/C/S text, so we are translating from the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stjepan Mesic continues, says in his meeting with

utterances.speaker: MR. TUDJMAN
utterances.text: "What is the most important for us?" That is what he says. "That had the Croatian diplomacy been good -- that it was good that they used all possibilities to portray Croatia in the most democratic of lights and now that is our advantage. And this is what he told me. He told me that because of that this is something that I can only relay to the president of the republic counting that it won't be -- it won't be related further."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph he says -- so Mr. Mesic is quoting the words of Mr. Andreotti; namely, Austria, Germany, and Italy would opt for a separate recognition of Croatia if that is not accepted by the European Community. "And I have already agreed when I was staying with him to meet with Genscher and I would do that probably tomorrow or the day after tomorrow." And yet a further part of this text that I'm interested in. Just a minute. Excuse me. Mr. Mesic then goes on to say -- that is page 116 of the B/C/S version: "But I came there ostensibly from Yugoslavia. Therefore, whatever my function may be, no matter whether it functions or not, it is from that position, nevertheless, that I stated that the only solution was to recognise reality." And then he goes on to say: "He says that we have obstacles being put in our way by Lord Carrington. He told me this in confidence. He said," he being Lord Carrington, also to Andreotti himself, "that he had heard from Milosevic that 27 Serbian villages had been razed to the ground, destroyed by the Croatian army which also expelled the Serbs, and that Milosevic had also said that he was not asking for an inch of land in the sense that it should be some sort of a Greater Serbia, that he was only interested in the rights of the Serbs in Croatia." Do you see that Mr. Dobrijevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time while you were in the territory of Banija and throughout the subsequent period of time, do you think that these facts that Mr. Mesic is imparting to Mr. Tudjman were something which really happened?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I, in fact, think that this corroborates my testimony in its entirety, including the thesis which I have not managed to adduce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you -- do you know when the Badinter Commission gave its opinion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date right now but I know of that occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is your opinion as a jurist and as a witness of the time? What is your opinion about the work of the Badinter Commission in the light of what Mr. Mesic says? Namely: "Andreotti promised to me that Italy, Austria, and Germany will recognise Croatia if the European Community does not"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I should like to reply to this question in more or less the same way as things unfolded -- namely, in the same way as things unfolded in 1941, they evolved in 1991. The same sponsors of the war and those who waged war in Yugoslavia then and now featured in Croatia again. So it is indisputable that the Catholic church, Germany, Austria, Italy, who were on -- that they were on the side of Croatia, and that is why Croatia decided to get rid of the Serbs, commit genocide against the Serbs, and make itself a state upon a genocide of the Serbs, because it is well known that after these events half a million of Serbs left Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. May I ask that this document be admitted into the case file. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note that we read two paragraphs of what is in fact a 100-page document. There are 12 pages translated in English. I'm not sure if the Defence intends to put in the entire document. I certainly would like to have a -- I certainly have not read the 12 pages, let alone the hundred pages. Perhaps this could be deferred until Monday, the admission of the document. I'd have an opportunity then to review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a -- you have the 200 pages [sic] in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, the translation actually comes from us. We did the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not disagree with learned friend's proposal that you rule on Monday, and if he hasn't had an opportunity to see the document, there's no reason for him not to do so by Monday. I must just note that we received this document from the Prosecutor under Rule 68 a couple of years ago as potentially exculpatory evidence. We received it from them and we translated only those parts that we deemed relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. He does say he's got a translation, sir, and he does acknowledge that you got that document from them. In that event, then, the admission of the document will be kept in abeyance until Monday when we will hear from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, maybe as I am from Austria, I am of course a little irritated by what you said about Austria being -- having been one of the sponsors of the World War II. Do you mean that, or was this a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when it comes to World War II, I can be more tolerant when it comes to Austria. But with regard to this year, absolutely not. You know that 23 MiG aircraft --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I didn't ask you to be tolerant but to be exact. Do you call Austria one of the sponsors of World War II? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The witness cannot answer the question with yes or no. Thank you. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, did you say this brings you to the end of your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I've concluded my examination-in-chief. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologise. Your Honour, Your Honour Moloto, with regard to what witness said and what His Honour Judge Hoepfel referred to, the Defence knows in 1938 there was the Anslauss of Austria. These are historical facts which fall outside the remit of this -- of these proceedings, and for that reason we did not insist on these questions any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It was myself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Judge Hoepfel, I don't think we should take it any further. I think we should bring the chapter to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- history and knowledge, and I said I had enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. The matter then stands adjourned until Monday, the 13th of November, at quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom II. Court adjourned.
